newsitem.title: UK: British train franchise faces big fine.
newsitem.headline: British train franchise faces big fine.

text.p: British railway franchise South West Trains, a unit of Stagecoach Plc, faced the threat of a one million pound ($1.6 million) fine and the loss of its licence on Friday in a regulatory bite-back after it cancelled 2,543 trains in eight weeks.
South West Trains (SWT), which mainly operates commuter services into London, has cancelled numerous services after job reductions left it with too few drivers to operate new shift patterns.
It faces the fine if it does not meet minimum levels of services in April and May. But SWT was confident it could improve its performance in time following weeks of misery for commuters.

After mounting criticism from passenger groups and politicians the Office of Passenger Rail Franchising (Opraf), which regulates parts of Britain's newly-privatised rail system, finally issued an ultimatum.

"Passengers on SWT have suffered an unacceptable level of cancellation in recent weeks. I am using my powers under the Railways Act to propose an enforcement order against SWT," said John O'Brien, Opraf's franchising director.
Transport Secretary Sir George Young described the regulator's tough stance as a welcome step. Stagecoach shares were down 21-1/2 pence to 735 by 1250 GMT on the news.
Under the order, if SWT fails to run at least 98.5 percent of services scheduled for April and May it would receive a one million pound fine.

If it fell below 97.5 percent of minimum services it faces a possible loss of franchise -- a damaging blow to Stagecoach and the government's privatisation programme just before an election, which is due by May.

But Brian Cox, chairman and managing director of SWT Trains, which has cancelled an average of 39 trains a day since February 15, was confident of avoiding the penalties. "We should be able to get services running again by Easter," he told Reuters, in time to avoid being "given the red card". Easter Sunday falls on March 30 this year.
Cox is also due to appear before the parliamentary transport select committee on Wednesday to explain his company's performance.
Asked about the commuter misery, he said: "We launched a new ship into stormier waters than expected. But we have kept our hand on the tiller and we hope to enter calmer waters soon."

But passenger pressure group Save Our Railways used the metaphor differently. "South West Trains was a flagship for rail privatisation -- it's barely out of the harbour and its sinking fast," said spokesman Keith Bill.
Stagecoach, which runs bus companies as well as rail franchises, already has had to compensate passengers who suffered cancellations, even without the threat of the million pound fine.

Cox told Reuters that the total bill could amount to 1.75 million pounds for the free tickets offered to angry customers and for refunds related to problems caused by signalling failures on the track network owned by Railtrack Plc's .
Railtrack is also a former part of state-owned British Rail, which was broken up under privatisation. ($ = 0.627 British Pounds)
